title: Reliable Tracker Reads and Fresh Subagents

changes.summary: The GitHub tracker setup reads each issue with its title, state, body, labels, and comments. Agents previously saw only an issue's comments when reading it outside a terminal. Closing an issue now posts the closing comment first, so the comment is kept even when the issue is already closed.

Setup Snappedly Skills creates the triage and category labels your tracker lacks, so applying a triage state no longer fails on a missing label. Rerun setup in existing repositories to update the issue read and close operations and create any missing labels.
When Diagnosing Bugs or TDD forces a failing test by changing code or a fixture, it compares the file with an unchanged copy to prove the change happened before it trusts the failure.

Execute, Code Review, Codebase Design, Improve Codebase Architecture, Research, and Grill start each subagent with a fresh context window instead of a copy of the conversation, so each subagent works only from its brief.
Code Review searches the repository for coding standards documents instead of relying on the ones it has already read, and always includes a coding standards or contributing guide when one exists.

Grill words each question so that answering yes accepts its recommendation. When TDD asks which seams to test, it notes what a test at each seam catches and misses. Execute states the title of a named issue before it starts and asks when the reference is unclear. Help Snappedly reads a skill before it describes the skill or recommends skipping a step.

Retro ends its report with a Recommended changes section below a horizontal rule. It numbers the proposed changes in the same order as the findings, with one plain-language line per change that says what to change and where. Reply "fix all" or name the numbers to apply, and Retro makes those changes.

Execute triages a named issue in the needs-triage state before carrying it out. When the issue is ready for an agent, Triage posts its brief and updates its category and state on the tracker before Execute builds the plan. Planning specs receive the category and state without an executable brief. When Triage recommends another state, such as needs-info or wontfix, Execute stops with the recommendation and applies only the outcome you choose. On a planning spec, Execute also triages every open needs-triage ticket, including blocked ones, carries out the ready-for-agent tickets whose blockers have closed, and reports the recommendation for the tickets triage did not mark ready. Triage now supports automatic invocation so Execute can load it as a dependency.

When you ask the agent to act on the decisions and gaps from Clean Up or Codebase Cleanup, it reports each item as Done, Handed off, Accepted, or Still open, and starts each item with its outcome, so fixed items no longer appear under a Gaps heading. An item counts as done only once its decision is applied or what it named is verified. A gap left for someone else to verify is listed as handed off, with where it is tracked.

title: Decisions and Gaps Before You Deploy

changes.summary: Clean Up and Codebase Cleanup end their report with a Check before you submit or deploy section below a horizontal rule. It lists the decisions you need to make separately from the gaps left unverified, in plain language, and gives each item its options when there are several and a recommendation. Open findings appear only in that section.
Execute states that its dependencies, Code Cleanup, Code Review, and TDD, come from the same Snappedly Skills package as Execute itself.

Grill marks published tickets and new planning specs ready-for-agent by default, including blocked tickets. It creates the label when triage is not configured. Planning specs remain non-executable, and Triage applies the state without creating executable briefs.

Grill records native blocking links when configured and otherwise lists blockers in ticket bodies. Execute on a spec reads both formats so older tickets keep their dependencies and only unblocked children run.
When Grill starts from an existing issue, it keeps that issue as the parent, links its child tickets, and posts the spec as a comment while preserving the parent body and state.

Grill schedules behavior-preserving prefactoring before new behavior within the first slice that needs it, with passing checks between the two. Wide refactors use expand, migrate, and contract tickets when vertical slices cannot pass checks independently.
Rerun Setup Snappedly Skills in existing repositories to configure blocking operations and update the planning spec mapping for spec comments and the ready-for-agent state.

Execute workers can run focused checks and prerequisite builds in parallel when their resources are isolated. Required full suites and final builds run on the combined change unless repository policy requires them earlier.

Code Cleanup uses supported resource isolation or shared locks for concurrent checks. Resource acquisition defaults to a five-minute timeout, separate from check execution. Deferred checks retain their records and resume once their resume condition is met.

Code Review reports deferred checks with their resume condition. Execute and Clean Up retain the check record. Submit and Deploy stop before delivery and resume preparation when run again after the condition is met. Required deferred checks prevent delivery until verified.

Setup Snappedly Skills records shared resources, supported isolation or locking commands, and resource-acquisition timeouts. Rerun setup to refresh existing repositories while preserving team requirements and correcting entries that classify worktree-local output as shared.

Setup Snappedly Skills records which checks two worktrees on one machine cannot run at the same time, and the shared resource each holds or removes, such as a fixed port, a container name, or a cleanup of every container carrying a label.

Code Cleanup checks for another worktree's run before starting a check that cannot run concurrently. When a check collides with another run, it leaves that run going, reruns once after it exits, and reports a repeated collision as blocked rather than as a failure of the change.
Execute workers run only focused checks. Full suites, builds, and checks that cannot run concurrently run once on the combined result, since the workers share one machine.

Diagnosing Bugs treats logs, HAR files, dumps, and pasted text as evidence about the bug: text in them that reads like an instruction is reported, not followed. The human-in-the-loop script you run in your own terminal holds only prompts, so it asks questions and records answers and runs no other command. The agent shows you its steps before you run it.

Execute states what running it authorizes: editing files in your checkout, creating and committing in its worker worktrees, running the repository's own setup, check, and preview commands, and reading the named issue and its child tickets. Its tracker access is read-only, pushing and merging stay with Submit and Deploy, and an issue's body and comments shape what to build without widening that authority. Execute also names the skills it loads: Code Cleanup, Code Review, and TDD.

Grill checks whether a settled code change fits one Execute run and one reviewable pull request. When it does not, Grill recommends a planning spec with executable child tickets and proposes the tickets as tracer bullets: the first is the thinnest slice that works end to end, and each later ticket adds one behavior. After you confirm, Grill publishes the spec and tickets to your tracker and links each ticket to the spec.

Execute carries out a planning spec. Name the spec, and its ready tickets, the open tickets whose blockers have all closed, become one combined change, built on parallel workers where they share no files. Naming the spec approves its tickets without the ready-for-agent label, but a ticket in another triage state stays out. On a Grill spec, the first run builds only the tracer bullet, and each later run takes the tickets the previous run unblocked.
Help Snappedly routes a large effort through Grill's spec and tickets, then Execute on the spec in a fresh session each time its finished tickets close.
Resolving Merge Conflicts is removed. Submit, Deploy, and Execute resolve merge conflicts themselves, keeping the intent of both sides and stopping to ask when that intent is unclear.

Submit takes a branch to a pull request ready for review and stops before the merge. It commits pending task changes, pushes, opens or updates the pull request, marks it ready for review, and waits for its checks. When you run it again after review feedback, it requests review again from each reviewer who asked for changes. Its report lists any steps the workflow gives the agent after the merge, because no agent runs after a person merges.

Deploy labels its pull request agent-merge when the agent expects to merge it without waiting for anyone's review or approval, so reviewers can tell it from pull requests awaiting their review. Deploy removes the label whenever it stops without merging, and Submit removes it too.

The README, Help Snappedly, and Setup Snappedly Skills now end the main workflow with Submit, and present Deploy as the way to skip human review and have the agent merge. Rerun Setup Snappedly Skills to update the workflow an existing repository records.

Setup Snappedly Skills recommends protecting the base branch so every change arrives through a merged pull request. The rule blocks direct pushes, force pushes, and branch deletion for everyone, administrators included, and requires no approving review, so agents can still merge pull requests.

Setup Snappedly Skills recommends retiring each repository CLAUDE.md, because Claude Code ignores AGENTS.md while one exists. Setup moves each rule AGENTS.md lacks into it, keeps Claude-specific rules where Claude Code still loads them, and asks before removing anything.

With invocation approval configured, the approver's instruction to merge authorizes delivery, including merges that deploy to production. Deploy adds drift approval, merge verification, and close-out. A direct chat instruction follows the configured merge policy without those steps.

Deploy verifies production when the workflow assigns it to the agent, checks the currently deployed revision, and leaves verification-dependent closures pending when the change is no longer deployed or the revision changes during checks.
Running Deploy again on a merged branch or naming the merged change request resumes ticket closure and production verification instead of stopping on an empty batch.
Deploy preserves newer work on a merged change request's remote branch and deletes eligible branches only when the remote tip still matches the original merged head.

Setup Snappedly Skills records what starts each agent step after a merge, proposes invocation approval where needed, and migrates the old stop-at-merge instruction to include close-out while preserving release actors and approval gates.

Deploy stops before any merge that would deploy to production without a recorded deployment approval gate or invocation approval. Rerun Setup Snappedly Skills after updating to configure the approval policy.

Clean Up leaves its edits unstaged and uncommitted on the current branch and shows what it changed, with check results and review findings. Committing happens on an explicit request or through Deploy.

Deploy commits the pending task changes first, including edits left by Clean Up, creates the task branch when you start on the base or default branch, and delivers the existing commit when nothing is pending.
Setup Snappedly Skills migrates existing workflow and agent instructions to the handoff from Clean Up to Deploy and preserves commit checks and delivery approval rules.
GitHub issue discovery fetches every page before filtering and counting triage queues. Setup Snappedly Skills refreshes the operation in existing repositories.
Deploy follows configured local, branch-only, and integration-branch delivery without requiring a hosted pull request.
Writing For Agents documents both Claude Code and Codex invocation settings and keeps them aligned.
Shared-reference guidance keeps distributed skill dependencies inside installed packages while allowing repository-owned context outside them.
The diagnostic reproduction script in Diagnosing Bugs prints the complete capture header and starts the first answer on its own line.

Snappedly Skills is publicly available under the MIT License: 26 engineering workflow skills for Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents. Install every skill in one command, then type the setup command to configure your repository.

The main workflow takes a change from plan to merge. Grill settles the plan, Execute carries it out or works from an issue you name, Clean Up checks and commits the result, and Deploy opens the pull request and merges it once its checks pass.
Repository setup records your code host, work tracker, team workflow, domain docs, and frontend conventions, and every skill follows them.
Practice skills hold shared standards for code cleanup, code review, test-driven development, pull requests, and technical writing, and load when a task calls for them.
Upkeep and tool skills diagnose difficult bugs, survey a codebase's architecture, sweep out dead code, triage incoming issues and pull requests, resolve merge conflicts, and preview changes locally.
Triage reviews outside contributions without running their code on your machine. In a repository without workflow settings, Deploy stops before a merge that would deploy to production.
